strengths: Interesting problem formulation: unifying architecture and weight generation into a width-agnostic multimodal sequence model addresses a real limitation of prior weight-space generative methods that are tied to fixed matrix dimensions.

The core empirical claim -- that GHNs with CNN decoders induce spatially correlated, locally structured weight tensors compared to unstructured SGD-trained weights -- is supported with clear qualitative visualizations (Figure 3, Figure 4) and quantitative nearest-neighbor diversity metrics that rule out trivial mode collapse (Table 1, Table 6).

The zero-shot width transfer results (Table 2) show a substantial and consistent margin over adapted baselines (SANE, D2NWG), and the paper includes reasonable analysis of why each baseline fails (fixed vectorization, unstable positional embeddings).

Reasonably thorough appendix with dataset generation protocol, hyperparameters, diversity histograms, and qualitative rollout visualizations, aiding reproducibility of the specific experimental setup.

The joint architecture-weight synthesis capability (Table 3, Table 4) demonstrating non-trivial zero-shot topology generation with high success rates is a nice additional capability not offered by baselines.
weaknesses: Critical missing baseline: since the training corpus itself is generated entirely by GHNs, and GHNs are explicitly designed to predict parameters for unseen architectures (Zhang et al. 2020; Knyazev et al. 2021), the paper never compares NNiT's zero-shot synthesis against simply querying the underlying GHN directly for the held-out topologies. Without this comparison, it is unclear whether NNiT provides any benefit beyond distilling/re-sampling what the GHN meta-model can already produce, undermining the central significance claim.

Very narrow experimental scope: only 4-hidden-layer MLPs, a width vocabulary limited to {16,32,64}, and three closely related simple ManiSkill3 manipulation tasks (all single-arm, low-dimensional control). Claims about scalability to 'billion-parameter foundation models' and depth generalization are speculative and untested; the paper's own limitations section admits depth is not evaluated beyond 4 layers.

The reliance on GHN-generated training data (rather than diverse independently-trained SGD networks) narrows the applicability of the 'structural alignment' finding -- it is unclear whether this alignment/patch-tokenization approach would transfer to weight populations not produced by a GHN, which is the more realistic setting for model zoos or real-world trained checkpoints.

Baseline comparisons (SANE, D2NWG) may be handicapped by ad hoc adaptation to a zero-shot topology setting they were not designed for, making it hard to assess whether the large performance gap reflects a fundamental architectural advantage of NNiT or simply weaker re-implementations of the baselines for an unintended use case.

The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (GHN parameter prediction, FiT-style flexible patchification, MoNL multimodal diffusion, DiT backbone) applied to a new domain, and the related work section is heavily padded with many only tangentially relevant citations, diluting focus on directly comparable weight-generation literature.

The impact statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks (e.g., of generative weight synthesis for autonomous robot control policies deployed with reduced validation).

No code/artifact release is mentioned, and given the complexity of the multimodal pipeline (dataset curation via 128 independently trained GHNs, patchification scheme, MoNL training), independent reproduction would be challenging without released implementation.

strengths: The empirical analysis in Section 6.1 comparing GHN+CNN-decoder weight magnitude profiles against SGD-trained weights (Figure 3, Table 1) is a genuinely interesting and visually compelling observation about the locality bias induced by a shared CNN decoder.

The evaluation goes beyond reconstruction-style metrics and actually deploys generated policies in the ManiSkill3 simulator, measuring task success/return rather than only parameter-space distance, which is a more meaningful test of functional validity.

The idea of unifying discrete architecture tokens and continuous weight patches in a single multimodal sequence (joint p(a,w) and conditional p(w|a) synthesis) is a reasonably novel framing that connects neural architecture generation and parameter synthesis.

Diversity/mode-collapse checks (nearest-neighbor L2 and cosine similarity) are reported for both the dataset and generated samples, which is a good methodological practice often omitted in similar work.
The limitations section is reasonably forthright about the restriction to shallow MLPs and the reasons for it.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity in the experimental design: the entire training corpus (6,400 'expert policies') is generated by an ensemble of GHNs (HyperPPO), not by independently-trained SGD networks across random seeds. Because GHNs already impose the structural alignment the paper's method exploits, NNiT is effectively learning to imitate/distill the output distribution of the very generator used to create its training data, rather than solving the harder, more realistic problem of generating weights that resemble the full permutation-ambiguous population of independently trained networks. This substantially undercuts the central claim that NNiT 'resolves permutation symmetry' for realistic weight populations.

The claimed 'width-agnostic' generalization is tested only on unseen combinations drawn from a tiny discrete vocabulary of three widths {16, 32, 64} across 4-layer MLPs (72 total topologies, 64 train / 8 test). This is a narrow combinatorial generalization test, not true generalization to arbitrary/continuous widths or deeper/wider networks, which makes the title and framing considerably more ambitious than what is actually demonstrated.

Baseline comparisons raise concerns about fairness: SANE achieves only 0-6% success even on architectures seen during training, which is a strikingly severe failure that suggests either poor hyperparameter tuning/adaptation of the baseline or an implementation issue, rather than a genuine architectural limitation; this makes the comparative advantage of NNiT over SANE less convincing.

No ablation isolates the individual contributions of (a) GHN-induced structural alignment and (b) patch-based tokenization within the NNiT architecture itself (e.g., NNiT trained on SGD-aligned or vectorized weights, or non-patch tokenization with GHN data). The paper only compares against entirely different baseline models (SANE, D2NWG), conflating multiple design differences and making it hard to attribute the reported gains specifically to the proposed mechanisms.

Scope and significance are limited: experiments are restricted to small MLP policies (≤4 hidden layers, ≤256 hidden units in the validation study) on three simplified robotic manipulation tasks. There is no demonstration on CNNs, transformers, or larger-scale networks, despite the introduction and future-work sections speculating broadly about 'billion-parameter foundation models' and general applicability.

The evaluation protocol selects the top-10 of 100 generated samples ('simulating an offline validation phase'), which can mask a much lower success rate in the full generated distribution; the paper does not report the performance distribution over all 100 samples, limiting insight into true unconditional generation quality.

The computational overhead of the full pipeline (training 128 independent GHNs plus an expert PPO policy plus the diffusion transformer) is not compared against the cost of directly training individual policies via RL/SGD for each target architecture, undermining the motivating claim that this approach 'bypasses the computational cost of traditional training.'

The Impact Statement is generic and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks of automated policy/weight synthesis for robotics deployment (e.g., safety of zero-shot synthesized controllers), which is a missed opportunity given the paper's focus on direct deployment of generated weights.

strengths: Identifies and empirically substantiates an interesting mechanism: GHNs with CNN decoders produce structurally aligned, locally correlated weight spaces (Fig. 3, Table 1), which is a non-obvious and useful observation for the field of weight-space generative modeling.

The patch-based tokenization scheme is a natural and elegant way to decouple generative modeling from fixed matrix dimensions, analogous to variable-resolution image/video diffusion transformers, and is well motivated conceptually.

The multimodal joint generation of architecture tokens and weight patches within a single DiT sequence (via MoNL) is a novel contribution that unifies NAS-like architecture sampling and parameter synthesis, which prior baselines do not support.

Experiments on ManiSkill3 directly deploy generated weights into functional robotic control policies rather than relying solely on proxy metrics, which is a stricter and more convincing test than typical reconstruction-based weight-generation evaluations.
Reasonable diversity/mode-collapse checks are included (nearest-neighbor L2/cosine similarity, pairwise diversity matrices in the appendix) to rule out trivial memorization.
Comparisons against two relevant baselines (SANE, D2NWG) show a large and consistent gap in zero-shot width generalization, supporting the central claim.
weaknesses: The entire training and evaluation pipeline relies on weights generated by GHNs rather than real SGD-trained networks; the paper's central trick (structural alignment) is partly an artifact of using GHN outputs as the data source. It remains unclear whether NNiT could generalize to natively SGD-trained or otherwise diverse weight populations, which limits the generality and real-world applicability of the width-agnostic claim.

The experimental scope is narrow: only 4-hidden-layer MLPs, a small width vocabulary {16,32,64}, and three closely related ManiSkill3 manipulation tasks. 'Unseen' architectures are still combinations drawn from the same fixed width vocabulary rather than genuinely novel widths (e.g., 48, 96, or depths beyond 4), so the strength of the width-agnostic generalization claim may be overstated relative to the tested conditions.

SANE's very poor performance even on in-distribution/seen architectures (1-6% success) raises concerns about whether the baseline was adapted and tuned fairly for this setting, which could affect the credibility of the comparative claims.

Reported results are based on top-10 selections out of 100 generated samples, which somewhat obscures the overall quality/success distribution of raw samples; a full distribution or unfiltered success rate would strengthen the evidentiary basis.

No code release is mentioned, and despite detailed hyperparameters in the appendix, reproducing the GHN training ensemble (128 independent GHNs) and full data generation/filtering pipeline is a substantial undertaking that may hinder practical reproducibility.

The paper's framing (title and abstract) suggests broad applicability to 'neural network generation' generally, but the method and evaluation are restricted to small MLP policies for robotics; extension to other architectures (CNNs, transformers) or domains is not demonstrated, which somewhat overstates the generality of the contribution.

The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with potential implications (e.g., dual-use concerns of automatically synthesizing control policies, or risks of deploying generated weights without verification in safety-critical robotic settings).

strengths: Interesting and testable insight that pairing a Graph HyperNetwork with a CNN decoder collapses permutation ambiguity in generated MLP weights, producing spatially correlated tensors amenable to patch-based (image-like) tokenization -- this is empirically supported with weight-magnitude heatmaps (Fig. 3), CKA analysis (Table 6), nearest-neighbor diversity metrics (Table 1, Table 5), and a permutation ablation (Appendix C.2) that specifically shows performance collapses to 0% when the alignment is destroyed, giving reasonably convincing evidence for the causal role of the proposed structural alignment.

The patch-tokenization scheme is a sensible technical translation of Flexible/variable-resolution ViT ideas (FiT) to the weight-generation setting, and the resulting width-agnostic representation is conceptually clean: widening a layer only adds patches instead of requiring retraining or new positional schemes.

The empirical comparisons against SANE and D2NWG on zero-shot (unseen width) architecture generalization show a large and consistent gap in favor of NNiT (Table 2), and the paper goes beyond a top-10 selection metric with the full 80-policy distribution (Table 9) and worst-case architecture numbers, which strengthens the claim that the gap is not simply a selection artifact.

The additional multimodal joint generation experiment (Table 3, Table 4) and the MNIST transfer result (Appendix H) provide some evidence that the approach is not narrowly tailored to a single benchmark or single generative mode.

Reasonably detailed appendix with dataset generation methodology, hyperparameters, and several targeted ablations (CKA, permutation ablation, per-architecture diversity) that support reproducibility and directly interrogate mode-collapse concerns.
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: since GHNs are themselves architecture-conditioned meta-models capable of producing weights for previously unseen architecture graphs (this is their original stated purpose in Zhang et al. 2020 and Knyazev et al. 2021), the paper never compares NNiT against simply querying the trained GHN(s) directly for the unseen topologies. Without this comparison, it is unclear how much of the observed zero-shot generalization is attributable to the novel diffusion-transformer patch modeling versus already being present in the underlying GHN data-generation mechanism that NNiT is trained to imitate.

The experimental scope is narrow: architectures are restricted to 4-hidden-layer MLPs with widths drawn from a tiny vocabulary {16,32,64}, yielding only 72 total topologies (64 train / 8 test). Depth generalization is explicitly not evaluated (acknowledged as a limitation), so the 'width-agnostic' claim is validated only for width, and only within a small, densely sampled combinatorial space, limiting the significance of the generalization claims.

The data-generation pipeline requires training 128 independent GHNs from scratch per environment plus extensive filtering (Table 7), which is a substantial computational overhead whose cost is not clearly compared to simply training conventional SGD policies directly for each target architecture; the practical efficiency argument for the overall NNiT pipeline (vs. just training networks conventionally or using the GHN alone) is not made quantitatively.

Evaluation relies heavily on a top-10-of-100 selection protocol for the headline numbers; while the paper does report full-distribution and worst-case statistics in the appendix (Table 9) which partially mitigates this, the practical deployment scenario of generating a single or few weight samples without an oracle simulator to rank them is not the focus of the main results, weakening real-world applicability claims for 'instant deployment.'

Baseline adaptation methodology is under-specified: the paper states SANE and D2NWG were 'adapted' to the zero-shot setting but gives little detail on how this adaptation was performed, raising some concern about whether the baselines were given a fair opportunity to succeed, particularly since SANE fails even on seen architectures (1-6% success), which seems like an unusually catastrophic failure that warrants more explanation/validation of the baseline's correct implementation.

Several forward-looking claims in the Limitations/Future Work and Conclusion sections (e.g., scaling to 'billion-parameter foundation models,' analogies to video diffusion efficiency tricks) are speculative and not supported by any experiments in the current scale-limited setting, somewhat overstating the paper's demonstrated significance.

The evaluation is confined to a small set of robotic manipulation tasks (three ManiSkill3 tasks sharing similar structure) plus a downsampled MNIST task (PCA to 32 dims), which is a fairly narrow testbed for claims of general-purpose 'neural network generation'; it remains unclear how the method would perform on more diverse network types (e.g., CNNs, transformers) despite these being mentioned as motivating related work.

strengths: The central idea—using GHN+CNN-decoder structural alignment to enable patch-based, width-agnostic weight tokenization—is a reasonably novel combination of existing primitives (GHNs, DiT-style patchification, MoNL multimodal diffusion) applied to a genuinely difficult problem (permutation symmetry breaking spatial locality in weight space).

The paper includes a battery of diagnostic experiments beyond the headline results: weight-magnitude heatmaps, nearest-neighbor diversity metrics, CKA representational-similarity analysis, and a permutation ablation that specifically breaks the claimed alignment and shows the expected collapse in zero-shot performance. This is a thoughtful set of sanity checks for the 'structural alignment' claim.

The zero-shot width-transfer comparison against SANE and D2NWG is set up fairly consistently (same expert dataset, same evaluation protocol with top-10 selection and full-distribution reporting in the appendix), and the gap between NNiT and baselines is large and consistent across three tasks.

Additional experiments (MNIST transfer, joint architecture-weight synthesis, single-topology diversity analysis) probe multiple facets of the claimed contribution rather than relying on a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The most natural and important baseline is missing: since GHNs (Knyazev et al., 2021; the HyperPPO GHN used here) are explicitly designed to predict parameters for unseen architectures, the paper never compares NNiT against simply querying the trained GHN directly at inference time for an unseen topology. Without this comparison, it is unclear whether the diffusion-transformer machinery is adding real value over the GHN generator that already produces the (filtered, top-100) training corpus, or whether NNiT is largely re-learning a capability the GHN already has.

The entire training corpus is generated by distilling a single multi-task PPO expert via an ensemble of 128 GHNs, and only the top-100 policies per architecture (out of presumably many candidates) are kept. This means 'generation of diverse functional networks' is really closer to approximate reproduction of one fixed teacher's behavior across widths, which substantially narrows the claimed contribution (joint generative modeling of neural network populations) relative to how it is framed in the abstract/introduction.

The architecture search space tested is extremely small: 4-hidden-layer MLPs with widths drawn from only {16, 32, 64}, giving at most 3^4 = 81 configurations, of which 64 are seen and 8 held out. 'Zero-shot generalization to unseen topologies' here means interpolating within a small, fully enumerable combinatorial grid, not extrapolating to substantially wider/deeper networks or genuinely novel architectures. This is a weak test of the 'width-agnostic... billion-parameter foundation model' scalability claims made in the introduction and limitations/future-work section.

SANE's near-total failure (1% success) even on seen/training architectures is surprising for a published, peer-reviewed baseline method and raises concerns about whether the adaptation to this setting was fair or whether an implementation detail (e.g., positional embedding handling) was mishandled; no sensitivity analysis or alternative SANE configuration is reported to rule this out.

The MNIST generalization claim, used in the abstract and conclusion as evidence the pipeline 'generalizes beyond robotic control,' is supported only by a single aggregate accuracy number in an appendix paragraph, with no baseline comparison, no per-architecture breakdown, and a non-standard 32-dim PCA-reduced input—this is insufficient to support the generality claim made in the main text.

There is no comparison of NNiT's generated policies against policies trained from scratch (via SGD/PPO) on the same unseen architecture, so it is not established whether the zero-shot synthesis actually saves meaningful compute/time relative to simply training the target network directly, undermining the practical motivation given in the introduction.

The paper repeatedly motivates the work with references to scaling toward 'billion-parameter foundation models' and general-purpose weight generation, but the experiments are restricted to MLPs with a few hundred neurons and simple control/classification tasks; this creates a sizable gap between the claimed significance and the demonstrated evidence.

The Impact Statement is entirely generic and does not engage with any specific considerations relevant to generative models of functional policies (e.g., potential misuse of policy generation pipelines, deployment risk if generated weights are not adequately validated).

strengths: The central insight—that GHNs with CNN decoders impose a locality/alignment bias on generated weights, converting an unstructured permutation-symmetric space into one amenable to patch-based tokenization—is a genuinely interesting empirical observation, and the paper substantiates it with multiple lines of evidence (weight-magnitude heatmaps across seeds, nearest-neighbor diversity statistics, and a CKA-based diversity analysis in Appendix C) rather than asserting it without support.

The permutation ablation (Appendix C.2), which scrambles neuron order in the GHN-generated corpus and shows zero-shot performance collapsing from 78.8% to 0%, is a well-designed causal check that directly ties the claimed structural alignment to the method's ability to generalize, rather than just correlating the two.

Patch-based tokenization of weight matrices (treating width as an image-resolution-like axis) is a clean and reasonably novel mechanism for decoupling the generative prior from fixed matrix dimensions, and the joint discrete (architecture)/continuous (weight) sequence modeling via MoNL is a sensible adaptation of an existing multimodal diffusion framework to this new domain.

Empirical results show a large and consistent margin over the two baselines (SANE, D2NWG) on zero-shot architecture transfer across three ManiSkill3 tasks, with supporting full-distribution statistics (not just top-10) in Appendix F, which strengthens the claim that the gap is systematic rather than a selection artifact.

Reasonable breadth of additional validation: MNIST transfer, joint multimodal synthesis of novel topologies with success-rate validation, and qualitative rollout visualizations, which together provide some assurance the method is not narrowly overfit to one setup.
weaknesses: A crucial baseline appears to be missing: since the GHN itself is described as already generalizing across architecture graphs (it is literally queried with the architecture graph to produce weights), the paper never compares NNiT's zero-shot weight synthesis against simply querying the underlying trained GHN(s) directly on the unseen topology. Without this comparison it is unclear how much value NNiT truly adds beyond what the data-generating GHN already provides, especially since the entire training corpus and its structural properties are inherited wholesale from the GHN.

The scope of evaluated architectures is narrow: 4-hidden-layer MLPs with widths drawn from a 4-element discrete vocabulary {16,32,64,input/output}, and interpolation/extrapolation is only tested within this small combinatorial space (72 total configurations). This makes the "width-agnostic" framing somewhat optimistic; it is unclear how the method would perform on substantially wider layers, continuous/arbitrary widths, deeper networks, or non-MLP architectures (acknowledged partially as a limitation, but the claim in the abstract/title is broader than what is tested).

The dataset-generation pipeline is very resource-intensive (128 independently trained GHNs, each requiring hundreds to thousands of meta-training iterations, followed by rollout-based filtering over tens of thousands of candidate policies) and this cost is not discussed relative to the alternative of simply doing more extensive search/filtering directly with GHNs or PPO-based distillation; a cost-benefit comparison would make the contribution's practical value clearer.

The gap in baseline performance is very large for SANE (1-6% success even on seen architectures), which raises a question about whether SANE was adequately adapted/tuned for this setting; such a large seen-architecture failure suggests a possible implementation or hyperparameter mismatch rather than a fundamental architectural limitation, weakening the comparison's persuasiveness.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: success rates are computed from only 50 evaluation episodes per policy and top-10-of-100 selection protocols, with no reported variance over multiple independently trained NNiT models (seeds), making it hard to assess how robust the headline numbers are to training stochasticity.

The claimed generality of the "GHN+CNN decoder yields alignment" mechanism is demonstrated only for this specific small-MLP control setting; it is not clear this generalizes to other weight-generation settings (e.g., CNNs or networks with skip connections) where previous GHN literature (e.g., Knyazev et al.) was originally developed for broader architecture search, so the applicability of the alignment claim beyond this narrow regime remains speculative.
